content.content:
95	--only layer,layer`, which selects whole layers, not cases within one;
96	`evidence` always shells `unit.sh`/`e2e.sh` with no flags, so it keeps
97	running every case.
98	
99	## Cases and fixtures
100	
101	Where the workspace has recordings, fixtures are **derived**, not typed:
102	`graphos-factory-core fixtures` builds every mapping from `.factory/recordings.yaml`
103	(case → sample), so a stub's request matcher is the request that was really
104	sent (base path stripped, repeated parameters as `hasExactly`) and its
105	response is what the API really returned. Re-record and regenerate; never
106	edit a derived mapping.
107	
108	Derivation also closes the sibling hazard that flat loading creates.
109	Grouped by method and `urlPath`, `fixtures` takes the union of the query
110	parameter keys *any* sibling mapping asserts, and writes `{"absent": true}`
111	into every mapping in the group that does not assert one. Without it a
112	recording that sent no optional parameter derives a matcher with no
113	`queryParameters` at all — unconstrained, so it also answers the sibling
114	request that *did* send one, and which stub wins is WireMock's tie-break
115	rather than which case is running. Deck-of-cards is the worked example:
116	`new_deck` (no parameters) now demands `jokers_enabled`, `deck_count` and
117	`cards` all absent, so it can no longer stand in for `new_deck_jokers`.
118	This is why a hand-written mapping is a liability — regenerate instead, and
119	if you must write one by hand, assert every sibling key you do not send as
120	`absent` yourself.
121	
122	A case is a GraphQL document plus its expected response:
123	
124	```
125	tests/cases/list_widgets.graphql
126	tests/cases/list_widgets.expected.json
127	tests/fixtures/mappings/list_widgets.json     # the WireMock stub that answers it
128	```
129	
130	The runner loads every stub once, before the first case, and leaves them all
131	loaded for the whole suite — only the request journal resets between cases —
132	so every stub is mounted flat for the whole suite, and a mapping
133	must still be classifiable as exactly one of:
134	
135	1. **Case-scoped by tag** — `"metadata": { "x-cases": ["list_widgets", …] }`.
136	2. **Case-scoped by name** — the basename matches the case name; hyphens
137	   and underscores are interchangeable.
138	3. **Explicitly shared** — `"metadata": { "x-shared": true }`, for a stub
139	   every case genuinely hits (an auth endpoint). Not for "several cases".
140	
141	An empty `"x-cases": []` is valid and useful: it preserves a recorded
142	response for an operation that has no case yet, classified but loaded for
143	nothing. Use it — with an `x-note` saying why — when a required argument or
144	a fixed pagination path makes a recording unreachable. Do not invent a case
145	the connector cannot send.
146	
147	A case-scoped stub may also carry `"metadata": { "x-required": true }`:
148	`e2e.sh` then fails the case, naming the file, unless that stub answered at
149	least one of the case's requests. "Some stub matched" cannot tell a case
150	whose connector ran from one the planner answered another way. `scaffold`
151	sets it on a `$batch` case's lookup, whose planner resolves the
152	entity's fields locally, and never calls the lookup, when the root
153	connector already maps them.
154	
155	There is deliberately no fallback. A mapping that fits none of the three
156	fails the run before any case executes, because unclassifiable loading lets
157	one case be answered by another case's stub while accounting still looks
158	green.
159	
160	Flat loading means every stub's `request` matcher must be unique across the
161	whole workspace: two stubs WireMock could both match for the same real
162	request are answered by whichever one WireMock's own tie-break happens to
163	prefer, never by which case is running. `graphos-factory-core lint`'s
164	`fixture-collision` rule (an error, not a warning — it means a test proves
165	less than it looks like it does) catches the exact-duplicate case: two
166	stubs whose whole `request` object is structurally identical, naming both
167	files. `fixture-overlap` (an error too) catches the *partial*
168	overlap: a stub whose matcher constrains a subset of what a sibling's does
169	(fewer query parameters or headers, fewer body patterns, the rest equal), so
170	it answers every request the sibling was written for. A scaffolded
171	`X_minimal` stub that names no optional query parameter is the shape: it
172	also matched `X`'s `?lang=` request, and the stub WireMock loaded last
173	answered. The finding names the `absent` matchers that settle it, or, when
174	only a body tells the two apart, a `priority` for the more specific stub
175	(lower answers first; a stub that outranks the broader one answers its own
176	requests, the broader one the rest). It compares every mapping, the ones
177	loaded for no case too, because a runner that mounts the whole directory
178	loads those as well. `scaffold` writes the minimal stub with every query key
179	it drops `absent`, and `fixtures` does the same for derived siblings.
180	
181	`e2e.sh` still catches what the rule cannot (two matchers that overlap
182	without one containing the other, `equalTo` against `matches`): after each
183	case it reads the request journal and fails the case when a stub that
184	answered is not the case's own (its `x-cases`, its name, or `x-shared`),
185	naming the foreign stub. That is how a connector that drops a query
186	parameter still fails when a sibling's `absent` matcher would answer it.
187	It loads stubs and runs cases in byte order (`LC_ALL=C`) whatever the
188	shell's locale: WireMock answers a request two stubs match with the one
189	loaded last, and under `en_US.UTF-8` `X_minimal.json` sorts before `X.json`
190	while under C it sorts after, so the locale used to decide which stub
191	answered and a run could pass on one machine and fail on another.
192	
193	Some requests are identical by definition — no field left to make them
194	differ (a fetch endpoint that sends no body at all, so its success
195	stub and its negative-control error stub can never be distinguished by
196	`request`). The only way to answer two such requests differently is
197	WireMock Scenarios: give both stubs the same `scenarioName` and each its
198	own `requiredScenarioState`. Spell the name with letters, digits, `.`, `_`,
199	`~` and `-` only: WireMock 3.13.2's scenario admin API does not decode a
200	percent-encoded name, so `e2e.sh` refuses any other name before a case runs. `fixture-collision` accepts a colliding group
201	on exactly those terms — same scenario, every member's own distinct
202	state — and still fails a group that only partly qualifies (no scenario,
203	mixed scenario names, a missing or repeated state). `e2e.sh` resets every
204	scenario to `Started` before each case (`POST $ADMIN/scenarios/reset`,
205	alongside the request-journal reset), then reads that case's own stub(s)
206	for a `requiredScenarioState` other than `Started` and sets it directly
207	(`PUT $ADMIN/scenarios/{name}/state`) before firing the request. No
208	separate per-case declaration exists or is needed for this: the state to
209	run from is already on the stub that answers the case.
210	
211	A runner that starts WireMock once for the whole suite and never resets
212	scenario state between cases cannot run a scenario pair: the pair would
213	depend on alphabetical ordering and stay in its advanced state for every
214	later case touching the same stub. A target that hands the suite to such a
215	runner says, in its own references, how a scenario member is marked and
216	dropped.
217	
218	## Pagination test coverage
219	
220	When an operation exposes a page-limit argument—especially when the inventory
221	declares a `maximum`—author cases covering: (a) a rejected over-maximum limit
222	and its error shape; (b) recovery that restarts at page 0 after a page-size
223	change (continuing at page N with the new size skips records in the gap);
224	(c) iterating to complete coverage rather than treating one page as the
225	collection (page 0..N, last page short or empty, assert the union of records
226	covers the expected set). These cases are not scaffolded automatically.
227	
228	## Copy and update test coverage
229	
230	When a write implements a copy or update flow touching a behavior-affecting
231	field (pinned, archived, visibility, status...), the case's body matcher must
232	demand the preserved field with the source's value — `equalToJson` on a body
233	containing `"pinned": true`, not an empty or partial body with
234	`ignoreExtraElements` (which matches anything; see the trap noted elsewhere
235	in this file). Prove the assertion is load-bearing: flip the demanded value
236	and confirm the case fails.
237	
238	## Scaffolding the tests
239	
240	Where the workspace has no recordings, the first draft of every test comes
241	from `graphos-factory-core scaffold`, not from typing. For each selected
242	operation with no case it writes the case document (every argument passed

245	matcher per query key, `equalToJson` for a flat body, a response built from
246	the inventory shape and carrying every path the selection names, however many
247	arrays it crosses; a branch the depth cap cuts keeps the properties its shape
248	requires, so the body still conforms) and a unit entry (scalar `$args`, the request, the
249	mapped response); a body-sending mutation with optional arguments also gets
250	its `_minimal` case. An input-object argument is sampled from the schema

252	object; the `_minimal` case keeps the required ones only) and a custom scalar
253	takes the JSON type of the wire slot it feeds (an `Int64` on an integer slot

input.message:
## lumen_books apply: done, with three gaps the tools report

The schema for all 11 operations is written and committed in the workspace's own repo. Nothing was pushed. Every layer that can run here passed: compose, unit, e2e, write-body proof, conformance, lint and JSON accounting. The open items:

- **Source coverage is not at zero.** `source-coverage --check` reports 3 of 11 operations failing, all on request-side `unresolved` rows (8 in total), with zero `unaccounted`. Details below.
- **Two relationship fields are not fully validated.** `Book.author` and `OrderItem.book` have no null-parent test.
- **Live and `supergraph_check` are `not_run`.** There is no `tests/live.yaml` or credential, and no graph ref or `APOLLO_KEY`. The subgraph has only been checked on its own, not against your supergraph.

Commits: `d8e0213 decide: patch openapi.json`, `b9aea9e apply: first schema…`, then `apply: evidence`. `lock --check` reported no hand edits before I started (no lock existed yet).

### What the schema now has
- **Query:** `lumen_books_books`, `book`, `searchBooks` (a POST under Query, per D-jnm0uf), `author`, `customer`, `orders`, `order`, `integration`.
- **Mutation:** `createOrder`, `updateOrder`, `cancelOrder` (returns `Boolean`, because the API answers 204).
- **Page types:** `BookPage` has `data, page, limit, total`. `OrderPage` has `data, nextCursor`. Every root field and constrained argument has a doc comment, and `ids` keeps the source's omission sentence.
- **Left off, as decided:**
  - Book `metadata` (new decision D-crbiq7)
  - Customer `email` and `phone` (D-xwq2hy)
  - Integration `apiKey` (D-nmhlzf)

  Each new decision records the omissions for source coverage and points back to the original decision with `--after`.
- **Entities (D-qbc6qk):**
  - **Book** resolves through a `$batch` lookup on `GET /books?ids=…&limit=50` with `maxSize: 50` (D-wnrxww). New decision D-x1ekw6 records why: `batch find` rates that endpoint as paginated.
  - **Author** resolves through a type-level `GET /authors/{$this.id}`.
- **Relationship fields (D-ox8zkp):** `Book.author` and `OrderItem.book` are pasted from `links apply`. `Order.customer` is declined in `selection.yaml`.
- **`selection.yaml` was updated to match the decisions:**
  - `searchBooks` root changed from `mutation` to `query`.
  - The two chosen links are confirmed and the customer link is declined.
  - The entity and batch flags are on `get:/books`, because that is where reconcile attributes the `$batch` connector.
  - The excluded fields are listed under `fields.exclude`.

### Calls I made that you should review
1. **`Order.payment` is one typed object** (`type`, `last4?`, `brand?`, `iban?`), not a union (new decision D-rvl036, resolved by me). Finding F-lr3c96, which said union, is superseded.

136 naming.md
# Naming

Every name in a connector schema shares one namespace with every other
subgraph in the supergraph. The prefixes are what keep two connectors from
colliding, and they are mechanical — `graphos-factory-core lint` checks all of them.

## The four names of one service

For a service whose directory is `widget-co`:

| Name | Value | Where it appears |
|---|---|---|
| directory / subgraph | `widget-co` | directory, `supergraph.yaml` key, schema filename |
| source / service | `widget_co` | `@source(name:)`, `workspace.yaml` `service` |
| type prefix | `Widget_Co` | `type Widget_Co_Widget` |
| field prefix | `widget_co` | `Query.widget_co_listWidgets` |

**The other three derive from the directory.** Snake-case the directory
for the source and field prefix, and capitalise each part for the type
prefix: `widget-co` gives `widget_co`, `Widget_Co_` and `widget_co_`. The
table above follows that rule. A vendor's own casing (`GitHub_`, not
`Github_`) or a short source name (`gsc` for `google-search-console`) is
allowed; a target that derives the names itself says what it needs to
accept a different one.

**The directory may be snake_case** (`widget_co`) when a consumer needs
the schema file under that name — the AppWorld benchmark bundle reads
`<app>.graphql`, so `simple_note` rather than `simple-note`. The schema
filename is always `<directory>.graphql`. `workspace.yaml`'s `directory`
accepts kebab- or snake-case words (`^[a-z][a-z0-9_-]*$`), and the choice
changes nothing else: the rule snake-cases either form first, so
`widget_co` still derives `widget_co`, `Widget_Co_` and `widget_co_`, and
rover gives the same `WIDGET_CO`. A snake_case directory is not a licence
for a CamelCase type prefix.

**Multi-word names use snake_case, never camelCase.** `rover supergraph
compose` derives the `join__Graph` enum value from the subgraph name by
uppercasing and replacing hyphens with underscores — `widget-co` →
`WIDGET_CO`. `@source(name: "widgetCo")` still composes; it just leaves the
subgraph schema and the composed supergraph SDL disagreeing about the
service's name, in a way that is easy to miss in review and annoying to
unpick later.

## Types and fields

```graphql
type Widget_Co_Widget { ... }          # {TypePrefix}_{TypeName}, PascalCase after the prefix
scalar Widget_Co_JSON                  # the one opaque scalar, if any
enum Widget_Co_WidgetStatus { ... }

type Query {
  widget_co_listWidgets(...): [Widget_Co_Widget]   # {field_prefix}_{camelCase}
}
```

`Query`, `Mutation` and `Subscription` are the federation roots and are
never prefixed. Everything else is.

Nested types take the path that produced them, so the name says where it
came from: `Widget_Co_Widget_Owner`, not `Widget_Co_Owner2`. If two paths
genuinely produce the same shape, share one type and record that as a
decision in `decisions.json`.

An inline (non-`$ref`) request body becomes an input type named after the
operation's `graphql.name` — `{TypePrefix}_{OpName}Input`
(`Widget_Co_CreateWidgetInput`), never a placeholder (`Input`, `Input2`) — and
an inline array body's item type is `{TypePrefix}_{OpName}ItemInput`. A `$ref`
body keeps its component name.

## Field naming inside the selection

REST payloads are usually `snake_case`; GraphQL fields are `camelCase`. Do
the rename in the `@connect` selection, not by renaming the API's fields in
your head:

```graphql
selection: """
channelId: channel_id
postAt: post_at
nextCursor: response_metadata.next_cursor
"""
```

Two exceptions worth taking deliberately:

- **Keep the vendor's casing when it is the API's own vocabulary** — an
  enum whose values serialise straight back into a request body should keep
  the wire casing rather than gain a `->match` translation table in both
  directions. This rule settles it, so following it is not a decision:
  record it as a finding (`graphos-factory-core findings add --cites
  references/naming.md`) only when an instrument needs it, keep a decision
  in `decisions.json` for a departure from it, and apply it to the
  whole connector. `graphos-factory-core lint` checks the other direction
  (`wire-enum-drift`): an enum value the spec does not list for the
  parameter or property it maps to, or a listed value the enum lacks, is a
  warning unless the connector translates it with `->match`. The converse is
  checked too (`closed-enum-as-string`): a `String` argument or
  field over a spec vocabulary of two or more values, every one a valid
  GraphQL name — declared at every spec property a selected operation
  reaches the field through — is a warning until it is an enum in wire
  casing or a resolved decision names the slot in `affects`.
- **Keep a name that is already `camelCase` on the wire.** Renaming for
  symmetry costs a mapping and buys nothing.

A snake_case field on a prefixed type, or a root field whose name after the
prefix is snake_case, is a lint warning (`field-casing`); a doc comment on
the field saying why the wire name is kept is the recorded exception.

## Operation names and the semantic root

The field name comes from `selection.yaml`'s `graphql.name`, unprefixed;
the prefix is added on emit. Prefer the name a user of the API would use
(`listWidgets`, `widget`, `createWidget`) over the vendor's `operationId`,
which is frequently copy-pasted from a sibling endpoint and wrong.

**Query vs Mutation is semantic and is never derived from the HTTP method.**
A POST that searches is a `Query`; a GET that mints a token is a `Mutation`.
This matters beyond taste: a POST is a write until the user says so. The
inventory records every POST as `semantics: write`, because a write
mistaken for a read puts a side effect under `Query`, where callers,
caches and retries treat it as safe, while a read mistaken for a write only
changes the schema's root. A POST whose name carries a read verb (`renderMarkdown`,
`/schedules/preview`, `repoGetFileContentsPost`) carries a `read_hint`, and
`inventory list` marks it `[read?]`. Surface every hinted POST to the user
and ask which are reads **before** writing `root: query` for any of them;
`selection.yaml` must carry an explicit `graphql.root`, `graphos-factory-core
lint` fails when it does not, and `read-root-on-write` warns on every POST
selected as a `Query` until `decisions.json` records why.

## Renames and collisions

- Two operations may not map to the same field name — lint catches it.
- Within one type, two source fields may not rename to the same GraphQL
  name.
- When the API has an `id`-like field, expose it as `ID`, not `String`,
  and use it as the `@key` if the type becomes an entity.

## Nullability

Be conservative. A field is non-null (`!`) only when the API is documented
non-null **and** you have seen it populated in a recorded sample or a live
probe. A mapped field the payload lacks yields `null` with no error — a
wrong `!` turns that silent null into a runtime error for the whole
response, and a spec that says non-null is not evidence: vendors ship
`summary: null` against a `required` declaration routinely.

Path parameters are the exception: their arguments are always `!`, because
the URI cannot be built without them.

## Scalar choice

GraphQL `Int` is a signed 32-bit integer. A source that declares a numeric
property or parameter `format: int64`, `uint64` or `uint32` is saying the
value may not fit — `uint32` is unsigned, so its upper half is past 2^31 too.
Past 2^31 the router nulls the field and reports a coercion error
rather than returning the number, and every offline layer stays green because
the recorded fixtures carry small values. The `int-overflow` lint
([testing.md](testing.md)) is an **error** on exactly this. Two fixes, and
there is no third — no doc comment silences the rule, because a sentence
beside a field does not change what the router coerces:

- **`ID`** for an identifier — a row id, a foreign key, or a resource's own
  number used to address it. `ID` accepts an integer literal as input, so
  `gitea_issue(index: 1)` in a test document keeps working when
  `index: Int!` becomes `index: ID!`, and the value is interpolated into the
  URL verbatim. This is the right answer for **an argument**.
  An **output** field is a different judgement: `ID` is for something a
  consumer passes back, not for a number it does arithmetic on, and this
  router hands an `ID`-typed numeric property back as a bare JSON number
  rather than a string — so an output that happens to be the same value as an
  `ID` argument still follows the magnitude rule below. The gitea pilot is the
  worked example: `gitea_issue(index: ID!)` and `Gitea_Issue.number: String`
  are the same number in the two positions.
- **`String` mapped with `path->match([null, null], [@, @->jsonStringify])`**
  for everything else — a magnitude (bytes, kilobytes, seconds, money in
  minor units) and an unbounded counter alike.

  The null guard is not decoration. A bare `path->jsonStringify` turns a JSON
  `null` into the four-character string `"null"`, which a nullable `String`
  field happily carries: the same silent wrong answer `int-overflow` exists to
  prevent. `->match([null, null], …)` hands back `null`;
  `$(path?->jsonStringify ?? null)` does too, but `reconcile` does not read a

input.content:
VERDICT: CHANGES

Schema review of `lumen-books.graphql` at commit 5cc3ca6 (evidence run 2026-10-21T18-50-32-418Z, commit b9aea9e).
The evidence input hashes for the schema, `openapi.json` and `selection.yaml` match the files on disk, so the evidence is current.

Summary: 1 blocker, 6 should-fix, 4 nits.

What is right: the prefixes follow `naming.md` (`Lumen_Books_*`, `lumen_books_<camelCase>`, enums in wire casing per F-jx72bt). Every resolved decision is carried out: metadata omitted (D-2hoz50, D-crbiq7), email and phone omitted (D-4yyj7v, D-xwq2hy), apiKey omitted (D-wf0vvx, D-nmhlzf), iban exposed as the user chose (D-a39c6a), Book and Author are the only entities (D-qbc6qk), Order.customer is not linked (D-ox8zkp), and searchBooks is under Query (D-jnm0uf). Both `@key(fields: "id")` fields are in their connectors' selections. There is no `@shareable`, which is right because no other subgraph returns these types. Output fields are nullable, which matches the factory's conservative nullability rule. Path arguments are `!`. The `@source` errors block surfaces `message`, `code` and `httpStatus`, and e2e executes every documented 401, 404 and 422.

## Findings

### 1. blocker: OrderItem.book bypasses the batched Book entity and fans out once per order item
- File: `lumen-books.graphql:166-187`
- `Lumen_Books_OrderItem.book` is a field-level connector on `GET /books/{$this.bookId}`. It sends one request for each order item. `lumen_books_orders(limit: 50)` returns up to 50 orders, and the spec does not bound the number of items in an order, so a single query can send an unbounded number of requests. D-wnrxww chose batching specifically so that "OrderItem.book and cross-subgraph references then cost one request per page, not per item". The `$batch` connector on `Lumen_Books_Book` (lines 66-91) exists, but this field never uses it.
- Fix: remove the field-level `@connect` from `OrderItem.book`. In the five connectors that return orders (`lumen_books_orders`, `lumen_books_order`, `lumen_books_createOrder`, `lumen_books_updateOrder`, and the items block of each), map an entity reference in the items selection: `items { bookId quantity unitPriceCents book: { id: bookId } }`. The router then resolves `book` through the type-level `$batch` connector, which takes at most 50 ids per request. Keep `book` nullable. Then re-run reconcile, lint and e2e (`order_items_book` should then hit `GET /books?ids=b-1301&limit=50`), and add an e2e case where an order holds two or more items.

### 2. should: Book.author duplicates the Author entity connector (lint `link-key-drift`)
- File: `lumen-books.graphql:101-117`
- `Book.author` uses its own field-level `GET /authors/{$this.authorId}` with a selection copied from `Lumen_Books_Author` (lines 121-137). Lint warns that the two copies can drift apart.
- Fix: map `author: { id: authorId }` in every Book selection: the `$batch` connector, `lumen_books_books`, `lumen_books_book`, `lumen_books_searchBooks`, and `OrderItem.book` once finding 1 is applied. Delete the field-level connector. The request count stays the same (Author has no batch endpoint), but the field then follows the single Author connector.

### 3. should: No demand-control sizes on the lists
- File: `lumen-books.graphql:10`, `141`, `209`, `260-271`, `331-335`, `407-416`
- `@listSize` is not imported or used. `BookPage.data` and `OrderPage.data` hold up to 50 items. `Order.items` has no bound. `lumen_books_searchBooks` has no limit argument at all, so its page size is whatever the API chooses.
- Fix: add `@listSize` to the federation `@link` import. Then add `@listSize(slicingArguments: ["limit"], sizedFields: ["data"], requireOneSlicingArgument: false)` on `lumen_books_books` and `lumen_books_orders`. Add `@listSize(assumedSize: 50)` on `lumen_books_searchBooks`, or a value from the API owner, and `@listSize(assumedSize: <documented or observed max>)` on `Lumen_Books_Order.items`.

### 4. should: Paging arguments do not carry the source defaults
- File: `lumen-books.graphql:264`, `266`, `415`
- The spec sets defaults for `page` (1) and `limit` (10 on both `/books` and `/orders`). The schema states them only in descriptions, so introspection and demand control cannot see them.
- Fix: declare `page: Int = 1` and `limit: Int = 10` on `lumen_books_books`, and `limit: Int = 10` on `lumen_books_orders`. The values sent to the API do not change.

### 5. should: Shared service credential exposes orders, payment details and customers to every graph client
- File: `lumen-books.graphql:18`, `template.yaml` (AUTH_EXPR test default `{$env.LUMEN_BOOKS_TOKEN}`), and fields at `194-202`, `386`, `407`, `456`, `484`
- Every request carries one bearer token. Any supergraph client can therefore read any customer's orders (`lumen_books_orders(customerId:)`), full IBANs (exposed per D-a39c6a), customer names, and integration webhook URLs. They can also create, update and cancel orders. D-wf0vvx also noted that `webhookUrl` may embed a token (line 229), and nobody answered that question.
- Fix: choose one and record it as a decision. (a) Set AUTH_EXPR to forward the caller's token (`{$request.headers.authorization}`, with the `Bearer ` prefix handled), so the API enforces per-user access. (b) Keep the service token and add `@authenticated` or `@requiresScopes` to the order, customer and integration fields and to the three mutations. Separately, ask the user whether `webhookUrl` should be omitted.

### 6. should: Evidence gaps to close before export
- `live`: `not_run` (no `tests/live.yaml`). Every fixture is hand-written from the spec (memory.md). In particular, D-x1ekw6 says the API's behaviour with `ids` and `limit` together "is not verified live". Record live traffic for at least `get:/books?ids=...&limit=50` and one order read.
- `supergraph_check`: `not_run` (no graph ref). Run it against the target variant before publishing.
- `conformance`: 60 bodies conform, 1 `unchecked`. Identify that body and either check it or record why it cannot be checked.
- Lint `missing-unit`: `lumen_books_createOrder` (line 502) and `lumen_books_cancelOrder` (line 594) have no `rover connector test` entry. Add them to `tests/lumen-books.connector.yaml`.
- Lint `link-null-untested` (lines 104 and 169): no e2e case covers a parent whose `authorId` or `bookId` is null. Finding 1 or 2 removes these guards. If either field-level connector stays, add the null-parent case.
- The Book `$batch` unit test uses one key (memory.md), and no e2e case reaches the entity connector with several ids. Applying finding 1 lets e2e cover this.

### 7. should: Payment input does not say which members each type requires
- File: `lumen-books.graphql:239-248`
- In the spec, `CardPayment` requires `last4` and `BankPayment` requires `iban`. The input accepts `{type: card}` with no `last4`, and the caller only finds out from a 422.
- Fix: describe each field: "Required when type is card." on `last4`, and "Required when type is bank." on `iban`. A `@oneOf` input split into `card` and `bank` is the stronger option, but it would reopen D-xghnp0.

### 8. nit: Mutations take flattened arguments instead of one input
- File: `lumen-books.graphql:502-506`, `553-558`
- The request bodies are the `$ref` components `NewOrder` and `OrderUpdate`. `naming.md` keeps component names, and the graphql-schema guide prefers a single `input:` argument. Consider `lumen_books_createOrder(input: Lumen_Books_NewOrderInput!)` and `lumen_books_updateOrder(orderId: ID!, input: Lumen_Books_OrderUpdateInput!)`. Do this only now, before any client depends on the current shape.

### 9. nit: List items are nullable
- File: `lumen-books.graphql:98`, `141`, `209`, `217`
- `[String]` and `[Lumen_Books_Book]` permit null items, but the API never sends them. This is consistent with the conservative nullability rule. Once live samples exist, tighten the items to `[T!]` (the list itself can stay nullable).

### 10. nit: Date and date-time values are plain String
- File: `lumen-books.graphql:99`, `158`, `212`
- `publishedAt` is `format: date`, and `createdAt` is `format: date-time`. Mention the format in the field descriptions, for example "ISO 8601 date (YYYY-MM-DD)", so callers know what to parse.

### 11. nit: cancelOrder's return value cannot be false
- File: `lumen-books.graphql:594-599`
- The field returns `true` or an error, never `false`. The description already says so. Consider returning the order id (`ID`) instead, so a client can evict it from its cache.
